newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portuguese government to present copyright bill.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese government to present copyright bill.

text.p: Portugal's Socialist government will present a bill to parliament on Thursday to defend copyright and enforce royalties for intellectual property, Culture Minister Manuel Maria Carrilho said on Wednesday.

"The bill to be presented to parliament tomorrow will aim to defend authors' rights that have not been protected due to advances in technology, such as photocopies of books, and copying of videos and audio cassettes," Carrilho told reporters.
The bill aims to implement a code to protect intellectual property rights that was approved unanimously by parliament in 1985 and reviewed in 1991 but not so far legally enforced.

"The copyright bill aims to implement article 82 of the Code for Authors' Rights, which establishes a payment (to the author) for the reproduction of audio cassettes, videos and photocopies (of books)," a statement from the Culture Ministry said.

"This payment is aimed at compensating authors, singers, editors, sound and video producers for losses sustained as a result of the reproduction of their works made possible by new technologies," it added.
Carrilho acknowledged that piracy of the works of international and local authors, composers and film makers was common in Portugal.
Practices include the sale in markets of cheap pirated videos and cassettes and in bookshops of photocopied academic textbooks, many of them written by foreign authors.
International lobbists for the protection of intellectual property rights had complained to Portuguese authorities about piracy, a culture ministry source said.
"We can't have piracy of intellectual property rights in a country that wants to develop," Carrilho said. "We are trying to rectify a serious problem."
He said the bill would not outlaw the photocopying of books, but added that companies that photocopy books would have to channel some of their profits to compensate authors.
"The bill is not prohibitive. No one is going to stop the practice of photocopying books. We are trying to enforce compensation for authors," Carrilho said.
He estimated that international and local authors, composers and film makers were now losing more than one billion escudos ($6 million) a year in royalties due to piracy in Portugal.
The ruling Socialists, who are four seats short of an absolute majority in the 230-seat parliament, were likely to get the bill passed, political analysts said.
More than 400 Portuguese writers, composers and film producers signed an open letter published by the local press on Tuesday urging parliament to pass the bill.
"We hope that parliament will pass the bill, putting an end to a situation that harms our interests as well as the economic and cultural development of the country," it said.
